correctness.rationale: For \(v\in V_i\), the signed Roman closed-neighborhood sum is \(W-\sigma_i+f(v)\), so all such inequalities are equivalent to the single minimum-label test \(W-\sigma_i+\mu_i\ge1\). A vertex labeled \(-1\) in \(V_i\) has no neighbors in its own part and is defended by a label \(2\) exactly when \(C-c_i\ge1\). These two conditions are therefore jointly necessary and sufficient. For each fixed profile \((a_i,b_i,c_i)\), the multinomial factor is exactly the number of labelings realizing it and its exponent is the common total weight, so the profile sum counts every signed Roman function exactly once. A fresh independent exhaustive replay over every multipartite profile through order six matched the literal vertex definition and the profile criterion.
residual_risks: The result is a profile-sum enumerator rather than a factorized one-variable product formula.

originality.rationale: The founding signed Roman paper and Zhao--Miao's primary complete-bipartite paper study minimum-weight parameters. A 2017 paper by Yin and Chen is specifically titled for the signed Roman domination number of complete multipartite graphs and is therefore the most plausible same-class predecessor. Public arXiv and open-web searches did not yield its full body; one authorized institutional retrieval attempt returned a transport error and was not retried. That inaccessible plausible source is retained as an originality risk rather than treated as failure. Current Resultary searches found no independent all-function weight enumerator, and the audited claim expressly excludes the known scalar minimum from novelty. Best-of-knowledge, the full coefficient profile remains additional.

value.rationale: Signed Roman domination is an established weighted labeling model and complete multipartite graphs already have dedicated scalar theory. The audited theorem classifies every feasible part profile and counts its multiplicity at every total weight, which is a natural exact distribution refining that scalar theory. The profile criterion is reusable for coefficient extraction and asymptotic or random-label questions, so the contribution is more than a recomputation of the minimum.
residual_risks: The all-function formula is algebraically direct once the two partwise feasibility tests are isolated.
